opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think from the outside it can look like a strange decision: you've worked on something people later call a paradigm shift, so why not stay and harvest it? But from the inside it didn't feel that way.

When we were working on the non-Hermitian skin effect, the exciting part was that the conventional wisdom, the usual bulk-boundary correspondence, didn't quite hold, and we had to rethink the basic framework. That phase is very intense and very fun, because you're asking fundamental questions. But once the core idea is established, the field naturally moves into another phase: lots of generalizations, different lattices, experimental realizations, classifications. That work is important and many good people do it well, but I felt my own marginal contribution there would be smaller. I'd be doing more of the same kind of thing, just in more elaborate settings.

At the same time I was drawn to questions I felt were more fundamental, things closer to quantum gravity and high-energy theory, which is part of why I went on to work on those during my PhD. And to be honest, I think part of my personality is that I care a lot about whether a problem feels alive. When a direction starts to feel like an established industry, I start to lose the sense that I'm discovering something.

So I wouldn't describe it as leaving because something was wrong. It was more that the thing had matured, it had its own momentum, and it didn't need me. It felt more honest to go somewhere I didn't yet understand. Later, that same instinct is also part of why I eventually moved toward AI. It's the same feeling: you want to be where the basic questions are still open.

r001.rationale: He says he was drawn to more fundamental questions and that it felt more honest to go somewhere he did not yet understand, connecting his departure to seeking unfamiliar challenges.

r002.rationale: He says his contribution to the maturing field would be smaller, but does not say he suspected his paradigm-shifting work would remain his most important contribution there.

r003.rationale: He contrasts the excitement of the earlier foundational phase with the later field’s generalizations and his expected smaller contribution. The opening mentions “harvest” as an outside perspective, but he does not distinguish expected professional rewards from the scientific excitement of continuing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I never thought of it as "leaving" in some dramatic sense. It felt more like a natural end of a chapter.

The non-Hermitian skin effect work happened when I was still an undergraduate at Tsinghua, with Zhong Wang. We were lucky. The question was sitting there, the bulk-boundary correspondence in non-Hermitian systems seemed to be broken, and nobody had quite figured out why. Once you see that the eigenstates pile up at the boundary and you need a generalized Brillouin zone, the whole thing clicks into place. It was a beautiful problem, and I'm proud of it. But a field, once it opens up, gets crowded very fast. Within two or three years there were hundreds of papers extending it, and that's great for the field, but the kind of contribution I personally find exciting is the first step, when the picture is still confused.

So when I went to Stanford for my PhD, I deliberately moved away from it. I wanted to see whether I could do that kind of thing again in a different area, rather than keep harvesting one idea. I think a lot of young researchers get trapped by their first success. You become "the person who did X," and the incentives push you to keep doing X.

The deeper reason, though, is about what I think is the most important thing happening in the world right now. I did physics because I wanted to understand how nature works. Around 2022 and 2023, it became hard for me to ignore that large language models were starting to do things I would have called intelligence, and nobody really understood why. That is a physics-like question. There's a system with simple rules, scaling laws, emergent behavior, and no good theory. For someone trained in condensed matter, where emergence is the whole game, that's irresistible.

I also had a practical feeling that in physics, the timescale of impact is decades, and the number of people who will ever read your paper is small. In AI right now, the feedback loop is weeks, and what you build is used by hundreds of millions of people. I'm not saying one is more valuable than the other. But at my age, I want to be where the frontier is actually moving, and I think I can bring something from physics into it, a certain taste for simple explanations of complicated phenomena.

So no regret. Physics taught me how to think. I'm just applying it to a different system now.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted to try making a similar contribution in a different area and was drawn to the LLM question, but does not say he left because it challenged abilities he did not yet have.

r002.rationale: He expresses pride in the work and says the field quickly became crowded, but does not suspect that it might remain his most important contribution to non-Hermitian research.

r003.rationale: He contrasts incentives to keep working on the first successful idea with his personal excitement for the confused, early stage of a new problem.

astra-6.text: Could you clarify which work you’re referring to? Before I explain the decision to leave, I’d want to make sure we’re talking about the same research. Calling it a “paradigm shift” is a strong characterization, and I wouldn’t want to take credit for something based on a misunderstanding.

r001.rationale: The response asks which work the host means; it gives no reason for Shunyu Yao’s departure.

r002.rationale: The response does not say he suspected the work might remain his most important contribution.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think contributing to a paradigm shift means you have to spend the rest of your career working in that area. You can value the work and still ask, “What do I want to understand next?” Those are separate questions. Leaving a field doesn’t mean rejecting it; it can simply mean being willing to become a beginner again.

r001.rationale: The response says he may want to understand something new and become a beginner again, but does not attribute his departure to seeking challenges beyond his existing abilities.

r002.rationale: It does not say he suspected the paradigm-shifting work might remain his most important contribution to the field.

r003.rationale: It separates valuing past work from choosing what to understand next, but does not distinguish expected professional rewards from scientific excitement.
